title: The Science of Learning Taxonomy
author: Build Cognitive Resonance
summary: The founder of Deans for Impact, who credits himself with popularizing the term 'the science of learning' through that organization's founding document of the same name, argues the phrase has become such a buzzword that it now means almost nothing, and offers a seven-part taxonomy to disentangle its competing usages. The versions range from his own preferred camp, grounded in a simple cognitive-science model of attention, working memory, and long-term memory (exemplified by Dan Willingham, Daisy Christodolou, and Deans for Impact itself), through a more granular instructional-moves camp built around Rosenshine's principles and Doug Lemov, to increasingly contested territory: Cognitive Load Theory as a standalone claim, explicit instruction as the sole legitimate pedagogy, and, most pointedly, 'the science of learning' as a justification for center-right education policy associated with E.D. Hirsch and former UK Schools Minister Nick Gibb. He is sharply critical of a sixth camp that ties the science of learning to neuroscience, quoting Dan Willingham's own dismissal of the idea that teachers need to understand brain function as 'a colossal waste of teachers' time,' and a seventh camp where ed-tech vendors invoke 'learning science' purely as marketing language, arguing flatly that you cannot fuse principles of human cognition into a software product. A lengthy FAQ section extends the taxonomy to the Science of Reading, questions why no equivalent left-coded science-of-learning movement has taken hold politically, and closes with a pointed critique of prominent learning-science advocates now contracting with the controversial Alpha School network.
points: Constructs a seven-part taxonomy distinguishing at least seven distinct, frequently conflated meanings of 'the science of learning,' from a narrow cognitive-science model of attention and memory to explicit instruction, center-right policy, neuroscience, and ed-tech marketing.

Names center-right education policy (phonics, knowledge-rich curriculum, explicit instruction, associated with E.D. Hirsch and Nick Gibb) as a distinct camp explicitly, arguing this version sets up an imaginary strawman of 'progressive education' that doesn't resemble any classroom the author has observed.

Uses Dan Willingham's own words to dismiss the neuroscience-based camp, quoting his statement that expecting teachers to understand brain function 'strikes me as a colossal waste of teachers' time,' despite Willingham's father having been a neuroscientist.

Flatly rejects the ed-tech-vendor camp by name, stating that claims like Google having 'infused the science of learning into Gemini' are marketing language rather than substance, because principles of human cognition cannot be fused into a software product.

Closes with a pointed critique of prominent learning-science advocates (Carl Hendrick, Becky Allen, Zach Groshell) now contracting with the Alpha School network, contrasting their optimistic public statements against independent reporting of Alpha School's academic failures and student attrition.
quotes: I bear responsibility for popularizing the term 'the science of learning,' and nowadays I see it being invoked in ways that bear little to no resemblance of what I intended. It's become a buzzword.

This version of SoL is deeply grounded in cognitive science, and specifically, a (simple) model of the mind that centers the relationship between information we pay attention to, working memory, and long-term memory.

Nick Gibb, a huge fan of Hirsch who served as Schools Minister in England, describes the 'progressive ideology' as including 'constructivism, discovery learning, and project work,' pedagogies he argues are mistaken because they promote the idea that the child has agency in the classroom.
As Dan Willingham once said, the notion that teachers need to understand neuroscience 'strikes me as a colossal waste of teachers' time.' Beware the many grifters in this space.

Google has not 'infused the science of learning into Gemini,' because you cannot fuse principles of human cognition into a tech product. But you sure can try to hornswoggle people into believing this form of 'science' supports what you're trying to sell.
